newsitem.title: THAILAND: Little relief seen for ailing Thai property sector.
newsitem.headline: Little relief seen for ailing Thai property sector.

text.p: Thailand's ailing property sector, now paying the price for rapid, haphazard expansion during the nation's boom years, will likely suffer more before oversupply is absorbed and the market picks up, analysts said.

The property sector has become the most talked about in the Thai market, getting blamed for the bourse's slump to 39-month lows and the recent decline in prices of bank shares on fears debt-ridden developers might renege on loans.
Industry executives and analysts say the sector is now paying the price for too much expansion too fast over the past decade when Thailand's booming economy grew an average of nine percent a year.
"We've had 10 years of unbelievable growth," said Simon Gray, managing director for integrated property services provider First Pacific Davies. "It's got to slow down."
The economy has already slowed sharply, with analysts recently cutting 1996 annual growth expectation to about seven percent from 8.6 percent last year.

Analysts said the ailing property market still has further downside due to the slowing economy and high interest rates. Oversupply, particularly of high-rise residential condominiums, will weigh heavily on the market, they said.

"This readjustment in the long term will be healthy," said Gray. "There will be some fallout in the property market, but developers who remain will be far more professional in the way they operate and the way they read the market."
Industry analysts agreed, pointing to the high vacancy rate in Bangkok's residential market as a good example of development gone wild -- with little regard to market demand.

"In the residential sector there is about a 13-15 percent vacancy rate in greater Bangkok," one analyst said. "Usually anything over 10 percent and you start to see various problems arising with the developers."

Gray said the current market oversupply will likely continue for 12-18 months. "If they stopped building everything today it would probably take about 18 months for the existing supply to work its way through the system," he said.
Although ubiquitous construction sites are still abuzz with activity, and jokes persist that the building crane is the national bird, analysts say fewer projects are coming on stream.

The slowdown has begun to hurt some of the smaller companies on fears of bad debts and poor profits. Other larger companies are shifting their emphasis away from condominiums to less-risky developments.
"There are going to be some bankruptcies throughout the property sector, focused on those who got high-rises wrong," said Neil Semple, analyst at HG Asia.

"The main worry is if a property company goes under how will it affect banks," he said. "Residential accounts for 65 percent of all property lending, and about 20 percent of all lending to the property sector goes to the high-rise sector.
Fears of an impact from property caused the banking sector to lose more than 20 percent of its value this month. Bank shares are heavily weighted on the Stock Exchange of Thailand.
The Thai central bank earlier this year warned financial institutions to be cautious in lending to property developers, in particular to those building high-rise condominiums.
